summary: Mexico lies in the southern part of North America. It was the cradle of ancient civilizations such as the Olmec, Maya and Aztec, and has the largest Spanish-speaking population in the world.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: After the Spanish conquest of 1521, missionaries promoted the conversion of the indigenous peoples on a large scale, and the legend of the apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe in 1531 fused Catholicism with indigenous culture, making Catholicism part of Mexican national identity. Although in the 19th–20th centuries the government strictly restricted the Church (the Constitutions of 1857 and 1917), even provoking the Cristero War of 1926–1929, Catholicism remains the faith of the great majority. However, its share has declined year by year from about 98% in 1950.

ranking.name: Protestantism / Evangelicalism
ranking.description: American Protestant missionaries began entering Mexico in the 19th century, but real growth came in the second half of the 20th century: Pentecostal and evangelical churches expanded rapidly in the indigenous and poor regions of the south such as Chiapas and Tabasco, offering community mutual aid and support such as help with quitting alcohol. Chiapas is the state with the highest proportion of Protestants, and conflicts between Catholic and Protestant communities have also occurred there.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The number of people with no religion in Mexico has increased markedly in recent decades, mainly among young people in the northern border states and big cities. Urbanization, the spread of education, frequent exchange with the United States, and dissatisfaction with Catholic Church scandals and political positions are all causes driving secularization.

religion.background: Mesoamerican civilizations such as the Aztec and Maya were polytheistic, centered on sun gods, rain gods and others, and practiced human sacrifice. After Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire in 1519–1521, missionaries of the Franciscan, Dominican and other orders promoted the conversion of the indigenous peoples on a large scale, fusing Catholicism with indigenous beliefs. The legend that the indigenous man Juan Diego saw an apparition of Our Lady of Guadalupe in 1531 embedded Catholicism deeply in people's hearts, and Our Lady of Guadalupe became a national symbol of Mexico. The Reform War of the 19th century and the 1917 constitution strictly restricted the power of the Church, and in 1926–1929 the Cristero War broke out. In 1992 Mexico restored diplomatic relations with the Vatican, and in recent decades Protestants and the non-religious have gradually increased.

language.official: Mexican federal law designates no official language; Spanish is the de facto national language, and 68 indigenous languages are recognized as national languages.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish arrived with the Spanish conquest of 1521 and in the colonial period was the language of administration, the Church and the elite. After independence in 1821 the state used Spanish to unify its people, and the education policy after the revolution of the 20th century further encouraged indigenous people to learn Spanish, so that the mixed-race population (Mestizos) speak Spanish as their mother tongue. Today Mexico has the largest Spanish-speaking population in the world.

ranking.name: Nahuatl
ranking.description: Nahuatl was the language of the Aztec Empire and was still widely used in the early Spanish colonial period, with missionaries even writing documents in it. But with the promotion of Spanish and discrimination against indigenous languages, the number of speakers fell sharply, and today they are mainly in rural areas of central states such as Puebla, Hidalgo and Veracruz. Words such as tomato and chocolate derive from Nahuatl.

ranking.name: Yucatec Maya
ranking.description: Yucatec Maya is a descendant language of the ancient Maya civilization, found mainly in the Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo states of the Yucatán Peninsula. In the 19th century the Maya of Yucatán launched the "Caste War" (1847–1901) against rule, and the local Maya language has been relatively well preserved to this day; it is the second most spoken indigenous language in Mexico.

language.history: Before the Spanish conquest Mexico had hundreds of indigenous languages, and Nahuatl of the Aztec Empire was the lingua franca of the central region. After the Spanish conquest of 1521, missionaries for a time used Nahuatl for evangelization and compiled dictionaries, but Spanish gradually became the language of administration and education. After independence in 1821, 19th–20th-century nation-building used Spanish as a tool of national unification, schools pursued a "Castilianization" policy, and indigenous languages shrank sharply. The 2003 General Law of Linguistic Rights of the Indigenous Peoples recognized 68 indigenous languages as "national languages" alongside Spanish. Today Mexico has the largest Spanish-speaking population in the world.

ranking.name: Tacos
ranking.description: A corn tortilla wrapped around various fillings such as grilled meat, stewed meat, fish or vegetables, topped with onion, cilantro and salsa. The fillings and sauces vary endlessly, and tacos are Mexico's most common street snack.
ranking.history: Corn was domesticated in Mexico about nine thousand years ago, and the Aztecs and Maya ate food wrapped in corn tortillas. The name taco may derive from the silver miners of 18th-century Mexico, who called the wrapped charges of explosive used in blasting a taco, a term later extended to food wrapped in tortillas. In the early 20th century Mexican immigrants brought the taco to the United States, after which it became popular worldwide. In 2010 traditional Mexican cuisine was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

ranking.name: Mole
ranking.description: A thick sauce ground and simmered from dozens of ingredients such as many kinds of chili, cacao, nuts, spices and bread, poured over chicken or turkey.
ranking.history: The word mole comes from the Nahuatl mōlli (sauce). The Aztecs had sauces made from chili, and after Spanish colonization spices, nuts and sugar from Europe and Asia were added, forming a fusion dish. Legend has it that in the 17th century the nuns of the Convent of Santa Rosa in Puebla, to welcome a bishop, made mole poblano from the ingredients at hand, but this is only a legend. Today mole is the dish for important occasions such as weddings, baptisms and the Day of the Dead, and the state of Oaxaca is famous for its seven moles.

ranking.name: Tamales
ranking.description: Corn dough wrapped around meat, cheese or chili sauce, wrapped in corn husks or banana leaves and steamed. They have a soft texture, can be sweet or savory, and are common at festivals and for breakfast.
ranking.history: The tamal originated in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, where the Aztecs and Maya ate tamales at ceremonies and in war because they were easy to carry and keep. The name comes from the Nahuatl tamalli. Today, on 2 February, Candlemas, Mexico has a custom: whoever finds the small figurine when eating the King's cake on 6 January, Epiphany, must treat everyone to tamales on Candlemas, an example of the fusion of Catholic and indigenous traditions.

ranking.name: Chiles en nogada
ranking.description: Roasted poblano chilies stuffed with a filling of meat, fruit and nuts, topped with a white walnut sauce and sprinkled with pomegranate seeds, showing the three colors green, white and red.
ranking.history: Chiles en nogada originated in the state of Puebla; legend has it that after the end of the Mexican War of Independence in 1821, nuns in Puebla created the dish to celebrate the visit of General Agustín de Iturbide, and the three colors green, white and red symbolize the Mexican flag. The walnuts and pomegranates it uses are harvested in August–September, so it is a seasonal dish around Independence Day on 16 September.

ranking.name: Pozole
ranking.description: A soup stewed from large corn kernels (hominy) with pork or chicken, served with lettuce, radish, onion, chili and lime.
ranking.history: Pozole originated in the pre-Columbian period and its name comes from Nahuatl. According to the records of the 16th-century Franciscan friar Sahagún, the Aztecs ate a special stew containing corn at sacrifices, which some scholars link with human sacrificial rites. After the Spanish conquest banned human sacrifice, pork was used instead. Today pozole is the dish most commonly eaten on the night of Independence Day on 15 September (the commemorative "Grito" ceremony) and at New Year gatherings.
